**Title:** Association of lipid-lowering therapy with dementia and cognitive outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

**Authors:** Catriona Reddin, Aidan Stankard, Kei Yen Chan, Finn Krewer, Conor Judge, Michelle Canavan, Daniel H J Davis, Martin O'Donnell

**Journal:** Age and ageing
**Publication Date:** 2025-08-12
**DOI:** 10.1093/ageing/afaf219
**PMC ID:** 12341882
**Full Text Available:** Yes
**Full Text URL:** https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12341882/


**Abstract:**
Lipid-lowering agents are effective in reducing cardiovascular risk, but their effect on cognitive impairment and dementia is uncertain. The aim of this meta-analysis was to determine whether lipid-lowering therapy, compared to control, was associated with a reduction in risk of dementia or cognitive impairment.

Lipid-lowering agents are effective in reducing cardiovascular risk, but their effect on cognitive impairment and dementia is uncertain. The aim of this meta-analysis was to determine whether lipid-lowering therapy, compared to control, was associated with a reduction in risk of dementia or cognitive impairment.

We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials comparing lipid-lowering therapy to control that reported dementia or change in cognitive scores, adhering to the Cochrane Collaboration Guidelines. A random effects meta-analysis was used to estimate a pooled treatment-effect. The primary outcome measure was incident cognitive impairment or dementia.

Twenty randomised controlled trials were eligible for inclusion, 15 trials (n = 139 169 participants) reported dementia or cognitive impairment on follow-up (primary outcome) and nine trials (n = 32 370) reported on change in cognitive score. The mean (SD) age of trial participants was 65.4 (5.06) years in the intervention arm and 65.4 (5.03) in the control arm. Lipid-lowering therapy compared with control was not associated with a significant reduction in dementia or cognitive impairment (1.33% vs 1.36% over a mean trial follow-up of 34.5 months; Odds Ratio, 0.96; 95% CI, 0.74–1.26). Heterogeneity was moderate (I2 = 37.6%). There was no significant association amongst drug classes (Statin; OR 0.90; 95% CI, 0.67–1.21, PCSK9 inhibitor: OR 1.77; 95% CI, 0.46–6.83, Other: OR 0.85; 0.61–1.17).

In this meta-analysis of over 100 000 participants, lipid-lowering therapy was not significantly associated with a lower risk of incident cognitive impairment or dementia. This meta-analysis provides evidence to support the safety of lipid-lowering therapy on cognitive health, however, does not provide evidence of risk reduction of incident cognitive impairment or dementia.

Keywords: lipid-lowering, dementia, meta-analysis, systematic review, older people

Lipid lowering agents (e.g. statins) are effective in reducing cardiovascular risk, but their effect on cognitive impairment.

Lipid lowering therapy was not significantly associated with a lower risk of incident cognitive impairment or dementia.

Our meta-analysis provides evidence to support the safety of statin therapy on cognitive health.

Cognitive impairment and dementia are a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, an estimated 57.4 million people were living with dementia globally in 2019, with a predicted increase in prevalent cases of 166% by 2050 [1]. Identification of population-level interventions to reduce the burden of dementia is a public health priority.

Vascular cognitive impairment is a leading cause of cognitive impairment and dementia [2]. Accordingly, interventions that reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) may be expected to also slow progression of vascular cognitive impairment, and there is evidence that blood pressure lowering significantly reduces the risk of dementia (relative risk reduction of 13%) [3]. Lipid lower agents (e.g. statins) are effective in reducing cardiovascular risk, but have not been reported to be associated with a reduction in cognitive impairment and dementia. Findings from observational studies have been inconsistent, with some studies reporting an association of lipid-lowering therapy and reduced risk of dementia, whilst others report an increased risk, the latter studies have been used to advance a case against statin use [4–6]. In addition, the association of LDL-C levels and future risk of dementia also appears complex, and may be J-shaped, with potential implications of an increased risk associated with low LDL-C levels [7].

Whilst prior meta-analyses of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating lipid-lowering therapy have not reported a significant reduction in dementia risk [8, 9], the sample size of the included trials were insufficient to detect a modest treatment effect of lipid-lowering medications. Since the publication of these meta-analyses, additional RCTs have been published, including those evaluating PCSK9 inhibitors [10, 11], providing an opportunity to update the evidence.

The aim of this meta-analysis was to determine whether lipid-lowering therapy, compared to control, was associated with a reduction in risk of dementia or cognitive impairment.

We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis, adhering to the Cochrane Collaboration Guidelines and reported our findings according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Guidelines [12, 13]. The meta-analysis was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO identifier: CRD42024514015). The data that supports the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

We systematically searched PubMed and Embase databases from inception to 28 March 2023. The search terms included are detailed in the Supplementary Appendix (eMethods 1). The reference list of studies selected for inclusion and published systematic reviews of lipid-lowering therapy were also screened for studies that met our inclusion criteria. Two reviewers (C.R and A.S) independently screened titles and abstracts. Full texts were sourced for relevant articles. Where data on cognitive outcomes were not reported in the manuscript, the associated record on ClinicalTrials.gov was reviewed. Inclusion criteria were assessed independently, and inconsistencies were resolved by consensus.

Studies were considered eligible if they: (i) were randomised clinical trials; (ii) included adults greater than 18 years with a minimum population of 200 participants; (iii) evaluated lipid-lowering therapy compared with control; and (iv) reported dementia, cognitive impairment and/or change in cognitive score and [v] had a 6 month minimum follow-up duration. Control was defined as placebo, usual care or no lipid-lowering therapy. Trials evaluating the effect of lipid-lowering therapy in a population with a prior diagnosis of cognitive impairment or dementia were excluded. These eligibility criteria were designed to allow the inclusion of a broad range of indications for lipid-lowering therapy to increase power, as it was hypothesised that if an association was present, it would likely be a modest reduction.

Data were extracted independently by two authors (C.R and K.C.) using a standardised data collection form. For each study, we extracted the title, year of publication, lipid-lowering drug (class, drug name and dose), control, design (open-label or placebo-controlled), intervention and control numbers, definition of dementia used, all-cause dementia, dementia subtypes, change in cognitive score. We reported outcomes from the point of longest available follow-up. One trial had two investigational treatment groups with a common control group [14], to prevent double counting and a unit-of-analysis error, we split the common control group into 2 equal-sized groups. Data were compared for inconsistencies and merged into a pre-final dataset which was checked independently by a third reviewer.

The primary outcome of this meta-analysis was incident cognitive impairment or dementia. We combined diagnoses of cognitive impairment and dementia in our analysis to maximise the number of available clinical trials. As cognitive impairment and dementia represent a spectrum of the same neurocognitive syndrome, our hypothesis was that any consistent reduction in incidence should be present for both conditions. The secondary outcome was change in mean cognitive scores (expressed as a continuous variable).

We used version 2 of the Cochrane risk of bias tool to assess methodological quality of eligible trials [15]. Two independent reviewers (C.R. and A.S.) performed risk of bias assessments, and disagreements were resolved by a third reviewer (M.O’D). If one of domain was rated as high risk, the study was considered at a high risk of bias.

A descriptive analysis of included trials is reported in Table 1. We calculated the odds ratio (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for each outcome of interest from individual studies. Weighted pooled treatment effects were calculated overall and individually for drug class; statin, PCSK9 inhibitor and other, using restricted maximum likelihood estimation to fit a random effects meta-analysis model. The variability across studies due to heterogeneity was investigated using forest plots and I2 statistics. For difference in cognitive score outcome, the mean change from baseline to follow-up was meta-analysed. The difference in cognitive test score change between the intervention and control group was calculated when the difference was not reported in the trial. A pooled mean difference, with 95%, CI, was estimated using a random effects model. Publication bias was assessed using a funnel plot.

Baseline characteristics of included trials.

A priori subgroup sensitivity analyses that assessed pooled estimates for trials that reported follow-up above and below the median number of months of follow-up, and including only trials with low risk of bias were performed. A post hoc sensitivity analysis excluding open label extension studies was also conducted. The rationale for this was to mitigate for ascertainment bias in open label extension studies.

The systematic search of articles published before 28 March 2023 identified 2526 results. After title and abstract screening, 346 articles were considered potentially relevant. Twenty RCTs, available as 62 articles, were included after full-text review (eFigure 1). Fifteen studies reported the incidence of dementia or cognitive impairment on follow-up and were included in the primary meta-analysis [6, 10, 16–27]. Nine studies reported change in cognitive score [14, 16, 19, 20, 23, 28–31], of which five were included for secondary outcomes only [14, 28–31].

Risk of bias was assessed in all trials which reported the primary outcome (eFigure 2–3). The overall risk of bias was deemed low in 10 trials [16, 17, 19, 21, 32, 33, 24–27], some concern (randomisation domain) for three trials [18, 34] and high (missing data domain) for two trials [6, 20]. Two trials were deemed to be high risk of bias due to missing outcome data [6, 20]. All trials were double-blind randomised clinical trials. There was no evidence of publication bias for the primary outcome (eFigure 4, Egger test, P = .65).

In total, 147 441 participants were enrolled, comprising 417 758 participant-years of follow-up. The mean (SD) age of trial participants was 65.4 (5.06) years in the intervention arm and 65.4 (5.03) in the control arm. 44 010 participants (29.8%) were women; 22 892 (30.8%) in the intervention arm and 21 118 (28.8%) in the control arm. The mean (range) duration of follow-up was 30.5 (6–68.4) months. The publication year ranged from 1997 to 2023 (Table 1).

Fifteen trials reported dementia or cognitive impairment on follow-up (139 169 participants) [6, 16–21, 32, 33, 24, 34, 25–27]. Dementia or cognitive impairment was diagnosed in 929 participants in the intervention group and 937 participants in the control group. Lipid-lowering therapy compared with control was not associated with a significant reduction in dementia or cognitive impairment [1.33% vs 1.36% over a mean trial follow-up of 34.5 months; OR, 0.96; 95% CI, 0.74–1.26 (Figure 1)]. Heterogeneity was moderate (I2 = 37.6%). There was no significant association amongst drug classes (Statin; OR 0.90; 95% CI, 0.67–1.21, PCSK9 inhibitor: OR 1.99; 95% CI, 0.61–6.44, Other: OR 1.35; 0.49–1.26). Meta-regression analysis showed no significant association of proportion of women enrolled with all cause dementia (P = 0.23) (eFigure 5).

Association of lipid-lowering therapy with Dementia or Cognitive Impairment. Forest plot demonstrating the association of lipid-lowering therapy compared to control with dementia or cognitive impairment. The squares and bars represent the mean values and 95% confidence intervals of the effect sizes, whilst the area of the squares reflects the weight of the studies. The combined effects appear as diamonds and the vertical dashed line represents the line of no effect. Int-Intervention, CI-Confidence Interval.

Seven trials reported Alzheimer’s dementia on follow-up (92 661 participants) [6, 24, 25, 27, 33, 34]. Alzheimer’s dementia was diagnosed in 52 participants in the intervention group and 64 participants in the control group. Lipid-lowering therapy compared with control was not associated with reduced odds of Alzheimer’s dementia [0.11% vs 0.14% over a mean trial follow-up of 34.3 months; OR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.56–1.17 (Figure 2)]. Five trials reported vascular dementia on follow-up (46 344 participants) [18, 6, 32, 25, 27]. Vascular dementia was diagnosed in 102 participants in the intervention group and 70 participants in the control group. Lipid-lowering therapy compared with control was associated with increased odds of vascular dementia [0.43% vs 0.30% over a mean trial follow-up of 38.3 months; OR, 1.45; 95% CI, 1.07–1.98 (Figure 3)]. In a post hoc sensitivity analysis excluding Anglo–Scandinavian Outcome Trial-Lipid-Lowering Arm (which accounted for 95.35% of the weight) lipid-lowering therapy compared with control was not associated with increased odds of vascular dementia (OR, 1.24; 95% CI, 0.30–5.21) (eFigure 6).

Association of lipid-lowering therapy with Alzheimer’s Dementia. Forest plot demonstrating the association of lipid-lowering therapy compared to control with Alzheimer’s dementia. The squares and bars represent the mean values and 95% confidence intervals of the effect sizes, whilst the area of the squares reflects the weight of the studies. The combined effects appear as diamonds and the vertical dashed line represents the line of no effect. Int-Intervention, CI-Confidence Interval.

Association of Lipid-lowering therapy with Vascular Dementia. Forest plot demonstrating the association of lipid-lowering therapy compared to control with vascular dementia. The squares and bars represent the mean values and 95% confidence intervals of the effect sizes, whilst the area of the squares reflects the weight of the studies. The combined effects appear as diamonds, and the vertical dashed line represents the line of no effect. Int-Intervention, CI-Confidence Interval.

Nine trials (n = 32,370) reported on change in cognitive score [14, 16, 19, 20, 23, 28–31]. Two trials, HPS and PROSPER, reported no difference in change in cognitive scores between groups from baseline to follow up, however there was insufficient data to include in the meta-analytic estimate [16, 31]. Amongst seven trials [19, 20, 23, 28–30], lipid-lowering therapy compared with control was not associated with a significantly difference in the standardised mean difference, from baseline to final follow up, in cognitive score (standardised mean difference, −0.09; 95% CI, −0.36 to 0.17) (eFigure 7).

A priori subgroup sensitivity analyses for the primary outcome that assessed pooled estimates for trials that reported years of follow-up above and below the median follow-up duration (eFigure 8), and a sensitivity analysis limited to trials at low risk of bias did not materially alter findings (eFigure 9).

On meta-analysis which included fifteen trials with 139 169 participants for the primary outcome analysis found no association of lipid-lowering therapy compared with control with dementia or cognitive impairment.

Our findings are consistent with prior meta-analyses of RCTs evaluating lipid-lowering therapy which have not reported a significant reduction, or increase, in dementia risk [8, 9]. However, our findings are more robust due to larger number of RCTs included and a four-fold increase in cumulative sample size. In the most recent Cochrane review, evaluating statin therapy, they included two trials with 26,340 participants. Our meta-analysis included 13 additional trials and 112 829 additional participants. Consequently, we add increased confidence in estimates for the association, and add to expanded outcomes by including both vascular and Alzheimer’s dementia outcomes.

Unlike some other vascular risk factors (e.g. smoking, hypertension), the relationship of lipids with brain health is complex. For example, an increase in low-density lipoprotein (LDL) is associated with an increased risk of ischemic stroke, but a lower risk of intracerebral haemorrhage [35], both of which are mechanism implicated in cognitive decline. There are compelling reasons to suspect a beneficial effect on vascular dementia, such as observational evidence which has demonstrated an association between elevated levels of LDL cholesterol and dementia risk, laboratory findings that cerebral AB generation is cholesterol dependent and identification of apolipoprotein E 4 allele which is involved in cholesterol metabolism as a genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease [36, 4, 37]. However, mechanisms whereby lipid-lowering might have adverse effects on cognitive function mediated through nonvascular mechanisms have also been suggested, and in 2012 the US Food and Drug Administration released adverse event information regarding cognitive impairment [38]. In this light, our meta-analysis provides evidence to support the safety of statin therapy on cognitive health. Whilst we do report that lipid-lowering therapy was associated with an increased risk of vascular dementia, this association was attenuated in a sensitivity analysis excluding open-label extension studies. During open label follow-up outcome ascertainment may have differed by treatment allocation, therefore this result should be interpreted with caution.

Evaluating cardioprotective therapies (such as lipid-lowering therapy) to prevent dementia presents more challenges than that for cardiovascular prevention. First, the association of modifiable risk factors (e.g. hypertension) with dementia is usually weaker than for CVD [3, 39], due to a lower contribution of vascular disease and greater contribution of other mechanisms such as neurodegeneration. Secondly, longer durations of follow-up are required due to lower event rates, especially for clinical cohorts with mean age in 60s. Thirdly, dementia was not the primary outcome of included trials, and therefore the sample size was not estimated for dementia effect, and low event rates related to nonsystematic identification of dementia incidence in majority of trials. This may be related to duration of follow-up. A commonly cited challenge of preventative strategies targeting dementia and cognitive outcomes is that there is often a lag phase between exposure and outcome (dementia) which may exceed the duration of RCT follow-up [40]. Ongoing efforts include the STAREE study and PREVENTABLE trial, which are evaluating atorvastatin 40 mg, compared to placebo, amongst community-dwelling older adults without CVD or dementia [41, 42]. The primary outcome is a composite of death, dementia and persistent disability and secondary composites including mild cognitive impairment and cardiovascular events.

We do not report on the association of lipid-lowering therapy with dementia by subgroups, such as by sex, as this data were not available. Prior meta-analyses of statin and PCSK9 respectively by sex reported similar cardiovascular risk reduction in women and men [43, 44]. However, statin intolerance and adherence may differ by sex [45, 46].

There are a number of limitations to this systematic review and meta-analysis. Firstly, the ascertainment of dementia outcomes may differ between studies, however this is unlikely to affect the relative risk. Dementia outcomes were not ascertained as an outcome of interest, rather they were reported as adverse events. Sensitivity analyses excluding open label extension studies were conducted to mitigate for ascertainment bias. Secondly, whilst dementia subtypes were reported by study investigators as adverse events there is limited data regarding the diagnostic evaluation conducted. Thirdly, the low event rates reduced power to detect differences in treatment effect. Fourthly, the duration of follow up of included studies was relatively short (mean follow-up 30.5 months). Fifthly, the mean age of included study populations were relatively young. Despite these limitations, we provide an up-to-date synthesis of available randomised control trial evidence of the association of lipid-lowering therapy with cognitive outcomes.

In this meta-analysis of over 100 000 participants, lipid-lowering therapy was not significantly associated with a lower risk of incident cognitive impairment or dementia. This meta-analysis provides evidence to support the safety of lipid-lowering therapy on cognitive health, however, does not provide evidence of risk reduction of incident cognitive impairment or dementia.
